paragraphs: This paper compares eight ways of turning images into representations for visual speech recognition. The central question is which image information should be retained before recognition takes place. The methods include different versions of principal component analysis and independent component analysis, combined with stepwise regression to select variables.

A key distinction is whether a representation uses statistics from small image patches or from an entire image. In the reported comparison, patch-based methods consistently performed better than methods based on whole images. This gives a concrete reason to examine local visual structure when designing these representations. The authors also describe the result as consistent with earlier findings on emotion and facial expression recognition.

The selection stage mattered as well: stepwise regression substantially improved performance by choosing variables and regions of interest. Together, the findings connect recognition quality to both the spatial scale used to construct features and the subsequent choice of which features to retain.
neurips-2000-a-comparison-of-image-proce.tldr: Local image representations and stepwise feature selection improved performance in a comparison of visual speech recognition techniques.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning models whose parameter spaces contain singularities, including layered neural networks and Gaussian mixtures. In these models, the Fisher information matrix can be singular, and the usual asymptotic normality does not hold. That makes the geometry of the model directly relevant to understanding its behavior as more data become available.

The paper uses resolution of singularities, a method from algebraic geometry, to establish a rigorous asymptotic expression for stochastic complexity. It then examines how the choice of prior affects that expression. With a positive prior, the authors report substantially smaller stochastic complexity than the comparison criterion named in the abstract, together with smaller generalization error than regular statistical models. The claim also covers cases where the model does not contain the true distribution.

The second case concerns Jeffreys' prior, described as independent of coordinates and zero at singularities. This produces the comparison criterion's form of stochastic complexity. The paper distinguishes its usefulness for model selection from its usefulness for generalization, showing that prior choice changes the consequences of singular model geometry.
neurips-2000-algebraic-information-geome.tldr: Algebraic geometry explains how singularities and prior choice change stochastic complexity and generalization in hierarchical learning models.

paragraphs: Non-negative matrix factorization represents multivariate data through factors constrained to have nonnegative entries. This paper analyzes two multiplicative algorithms for finding such factors. Their update rules look very similar: each changes the current factors by multiplication, and the algorithms differ only slightly in the multiplier they use.

That small difference corresponds to a different measure of reconstruction quality. One algorithm minimizes conventional least squares error, while the other minimizes generalized Kullback–Leibler divergence. The analysis therefore connects each update rule to a particular optimization objective, giving a mathematical explanation for what the algorithm is trying to improve.

The authors prove monotonic convergence using an auxiliary function, following an approach analogous to convergence proofs for expectation-maximization. They also interpret both algorithms as gradient descent with a separate rescaling for different coordinates. Those rescaling factors are chosen to ensure convergence. These two views explain both why the multiplicative updates improve their respective objectives and how they relate to a familiar optimization framework.
neurips-2000-algorithms-for-non-negative.tldr: Two multiplicative NMF algorithms optimize different reconstruction objectives, with monotonic convergence explained through auxiliary functions and rescaled gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how often multiuser demodulators recover transmitted bits incorrectly in a direct-sequence CDMA channel. The setting uses binary phase-shift keying and additive Gaussian noise. Its focus is the performance of demodulation methods when multiple users share the channel under these stated signal and noise assumptions.

The authors express demodulation as a finite-temperature decoding problem and use replica analysis to evaluate marginal posterior mode demodulators. This family includes the optimal demodulator and the maximum a posteriori demodulator as special cases. The formulation places several decoding choices within one analytical framework, allowing their bit-error behavior to be studied through the same approach.

The paper also proposes an approximate implementation using an analog-valued Hopfield model as a naive mean-field approximation. Replica analysis evaluates this implementation as well. The reported results favor both the optimal and mean-field demodulators over the conventional method, especially at small information bit rates and low noise levels. The approximate implementation thus accompanies the theoretical analysis with a concrete computational proposal.
neurips-2000-analysis-of-bit-error-proba.tldr: Replica analysis supports optimal and mean-field CDMA demodulators over a conventional method, especially at low bit rates and noise levels.

paragraphs: This paper examines reinforcement learning problems in which feedback has several numerical components. An agent may pursue multiple goals or serve multiple users, so its rewards naturally come from more than one source. The learning problem must therefore account for several pieces of evaluative information about the agent's behavior.

The authors argue that combining these components into a single reward can discard information that is important to the solution. Once different sources have been merged, the learner may lose distinctions that matter to the original problem. The abstract states that this can lead to incorrect solutions, making reward representation a substantive part of the learning problem.

The paper describes this multiple-reward setting, discusses difficulties with applying traditional reinforcement learning, and introduces an algorithm for finding a solution. It also presents results in simulated environments. The contribution is to treat multiple reward sources explicitly and connect that formulation to a learning method, rather than assume that producing one combined number fully preserves the task.
neurips-2000-balancing-multiple-sources-.tldr: The paper introduces an algorithm for reinforcement learning with multiple reward sources, where combining rewards can lose essential information.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis separates signals using assumptions that may not match real-world recordings. This paper introduces an algorithm that supplements those assumptions with information from the recognition task. Its form of top-down selective attention lets a classifier influence the signals recovered by the ICA network.

The method adds a multilayer perceptron classifier to a separated signal channel and sends the classifier's error backward through the ICA network. This feedback estimates an expected ICA output for attention. The unmixing matrix is then retrained with a cost function that accounts for both the classification error and independence, connecting signal separation directly to what the recognizer needs.

The resulting adjustment changes the distribution of recovered signals toward one suitable for classification. On noisy speech recorded in real environments, the authors report improved recognition and robustness to parameter changes. The stated finding supports using task feedback to compensate for mismatches in ICA assumptions, with the separation stage and recognition stage influencing one another through the learning procedure.
neurips-2000-combining-ica-and-top-down-.tldr: Feeding speech-classifier errors back into ICA improved recognition of real noisy recordings and robustness to parameter changes.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a distance-based clustering method that combines pairwise relationships with vector quantization. Its starting point is a matrix of distances between data items. The method turns that matrix into a Markov process, making clustering a question about how information changes as a probabilistic process evolves.

During the process's relaxation, the method examines the decline in mutual information about the starting point. Clusters appear as structures that remain relatively stable while the overall process relaxes. This supplies an interpretation of a cluster: it is a grouping that persists in the dynamics and retains information about where those dynamics began.

The information bottleneck method then extracts these groupings to capture information about the initial point as effectively as possible. The authors describe the approach as nonparametric and requiring no assumption about the underlying distribution or imposed geometric bias. Its central contribution is the connection between distances, temporal persistence, and information preservation, which gives the resulting clusters a meaning tied to the constructed process.
neurips-2000-data-clustering-by-markovia.tldr: The method finds clusters as persistent structures in a distance-derived Markov process and extracts them through the information bottleneck.

paragraphs: Explaining away is usually discussed as an inference effect involving the hidden states of a belief network. This paper shows that it can also occur when Bayesian inference concerns the weights of relationships. The application is conditioning, where the weights describe associations between stimuli and reinforcers.

The authors extend a Kalman filter model to account for explaining away in this weight space. They also offer an approximate interpretation of the Kalman gain matrix as a whitener for the correlation matrix of the observation process. In plain language, this connects the learning update to a transformation that addresses correlations in the observations, giving another way to understand how evidence changes the inferred relationships.

The paper suggests a network implementation of this whitening operation using an architecture attributed to Goodall. The resulting model exhibits backward blocking, the conditioning phenomenon motivating the analysis. The contribution links a Bayesian account of changing associative weights, an approximate mathematical interpretation of the update, and a proposed network realization within one model.
neurips-2000-explaining-away-in-weight-s.tldr: An extended Kalman filter model shows how explaining away among associative weights can produce backward blocking.

paragraphs: Different synapses can respond differently to exactly the same sequence of incoming spikes. The abstract describes this heterogeneity in terms of the amplitudes of successive postsynaptic responses. The paper asks how to characterize the input that best suits a particular synapse, given its individual dynamics.

The authors develop methods for computing an optimally fitted spike train when the synapse's parameters are known. One stated objective is to maximize the sum of postsynaptic responses. This turns a general question about synaptic function into a specific optimization problem: for the modeled synapse and chosen objective, identify the timing pattern that produces the strongest desired response.

The reported finding is that most of these optimized spike trains resemble common firing patterns associated with particular neuron types in the literature. That correspondence connects the computed inputs with patterns already discussed in neuroscience. The work provides a concrete way to investigate synaptic heterogeneity by relating each synapse's known parameters to the spike sequences it responds to most effectively.
neurips-2000-finding-the-key-to-a-synaps.tldr: Computed spike trains optimized for individual synapses often resemble common firing patterns of specific neuron types.

paragraphs: Output coding solves a multiclass classification problem by expressing it through several binary classification problems. The code determines how these binary tasks represent the original classes. This paper focuses on improving that representation, observing that previous output-coding research had relied almost entirely on predefined discrete codes.

The proposed algorithm relaxes the codes into continuous values and treats their improvement as an optimization problem. This permits adjustments beyond the choices available in the original discrete representation. The authors describe the resulting optimization as reminiscent of the quadratic program used for support vector machines, connecting code design to an established style of classification optimization.

Experiments compare the proposed approach with standard discrete output codes. The results indicate that continuous relaxation often improves generalization, with especially noticeable benefits for short codes. The finding makes the code itself an object of optimization within multiclass learning. Its empirical qualification matters: the reported improvement is frequent in the experiments, and particularly associated with short codes, rather than stated as a universal guarantee.
neurips-2000-improved-output-coding-for-.tldr: Optimizing continuous relaxations of output codes often improved multiclass generalization in experiments, especially for short codes.

paragraphs: Active contours represent shapes that must be tracked across video frames. The paper addresses cases where those shapes are highly flexible, such as contours following fingers. Although condensation particle filtering had worked for strongly constrained contours, the abstract explains that flexible shapes require a computationally burdensome number of particles to approximate their distribution successfully.

The proposed method uses the Metropolis algorithm to update a collection of particles representing possible contours at each frame. Its focus is therefore the procedure for maintaining a distribution over shapes as the video progresses. By changing how the particle set is updated, the method addresses the difficulty of representing substantial shape variation.

The authors compare the approach with condensation on a video sequence requiring highly flexible contours and report dramatically better performance. They also discuss incorporating the method into an active-contour framework that constrains variation through a shape subspace. The stated comparison supports Metropolis updates for the demanding sequence studied, while the framework discussion connects those updates with explicit restrictions on possible shapes.
neurips-2000-keeping-flexible-active-con.tldr: Metropolis updates substantially improved flexible-contour tracking over condensation in the reported video comparison.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn a smooth probability density without restricting it to a model with a fixed, finite set of parameters. The problem still requires balancing fit to the observations against complexity. The authors numerically implement a prior based on quantum field theory to regulate the possible density functions.

A central result is that the theory's smoothness scale can be determined consistently from the data. This makes the amount of smoothing part of the inference problem. The authors interpret the procedure as an infinite-dimensional extension of the minimum description length principle, connecting density estimation to a balance between explanatory fit and the complexity of the representation.

The numerical investigation also examines the effects of choosing a prior and a parameterization. The authors conclude that determining the smoothness scale makes density estimates only weakly sensitive to the prior choice. They further find that even unsuitable choices can help with small datasets. These findings describe how adaptive smoothing changes the practical influence of prior assumptions in the setting studied.
neurips-2000-learning-continuous-distrib.tldr: Numerical field-theoretic density estimation learns its smoothness scale from data and shows weak sensitivity to prior choice.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to approximate average-case learning curves for Gaussian process regression. A learning curve describes how learning performance changes with the amount of training data. The average-case focus concerns behavior across datasets, making the target a broader description of learning than the result obtained from one particular sample.

The approach draws on statistical mechanics to make these curves approximately computable. The authors state that the approximation works well in the limit of large sample sizes and accommodates arbitrary input dimensionality. Those are distinct aspects of the claim: dimensionality is unrestricted, while the stated favorable accuracy concerns the large-sample regime.

The paper also explains how to improve the approximation systematically. This gives the framework a route to refinement beyond its initial approximation. Finally, the authors argue that related techniques could apply to general likelihood models. That proposed extension broadens the potential relevance of the approach, while the concrete method described in the abstract addresses learning curves for Gaussian process regression.
neurips-2000-learning-curves-for-gaussia.tldr: A statistical-mechanics framework approximates Gaussian process learning curves, works well at large sample sizes, and permits systematic refinement.

paragraphs: This paper adapts wavelet representations to encode natural images with sparse coefficients. The representation is built from a small collection of spatial functions repeated across image locations and combined recursively across scales. This architecture preserves a self-similar structure while allowing the functions themselves to be learned from images.

Learning minimizes an estimated code length under a model in which images are linear combinations of sparse, independent components. The basis can be complete or overcomplete, allowing the study to examine both forms within the same architecture. The objective ties the learned visual structure to how efficiently the model represents the image data.

When trained on natural images, the functions develop different orientations that evenly cover the orientation domain. The authors contrast this with standard non-oriented wavelet bases used in image compression. When overcompleteness is allowed, the learned representation also achieves higher coding efficiency than standard wavelets. The findings connect adaptation to both the organization of image features and an improvement in the efficiency of their representation.
neurips-2000-learning-sparse-image-codes.tldr: Learning wavelet functions from natural images produces evenly distributed orientations and, with overcompleteness, better coding efficiency than standard wavelets.

paragraphs: This paper explores image-sequence recognition with partially observable stochastic differential equation models. The models describe evolving dynamics whose state is not fully observed through the images. Their proposed attraction for sequence recognition is the use of continuous state dynamics, which the authors identify as a potential advantage over hidden Markov models.

To learn and evaluate these models, the authors use Monte Carlo importance sampling to estimate sequence likelihoods and their gradients efficiently. The likelihood measures how well a model accounts for a sequence, while its gradient supplies information for learning the network dynamics. These estimates make the dynamical formulation usable within the proposed recognition framework.

After learning the dynamics, the SDE models are applied to recognition in a manner similar to the common use of hidden Markov models. The authors report encouraging results on a video-sequence recognition task, describing excellent performance in comparison with HMMs. The reported experiment supports the framework's promise, while continuous dynamics remain the stated potential reason for preferring this model family.
neurips-2000-partially-observable-sde-mo.tldr: Partially observable SDE models use importance sampling for learning and show encouraging video-recognition performance compared with HMMs.

paragraphs: This paper introduces periodic component analysis, an eigenvalue method for representing periodic structure in speech. It analyzes signals through matrix diagonalization, with a mathematical form reminiscent of principal component analysis and independent component analysis. The intended separation is between periodic spectral components and noise.

The method uses constructive interference to strengthen periodic components and destructive interference to cancel noise. Its front end also emulates aspects of auditory processing, including cochlear filtering, nonlinear compression, and insensitivity to phase. These choices are motivated by the goal of approaching human listeners' robustness, rather than presented as proof that the goal has been reached.

The authors identify computational advantages over autocorrelation at the pitch period. Their method avoids long delay lines and correlates signals at a clock rate comparable to the pitch, rather than the original sampling rate. The paper derives the cost function and presents experimental results. Together, these contributions connect a periodicity-focused representation with an auditory-inspired front end and a more economical timing structure for correlation.
neurips-2000-periodic-component-analysis.tldr: Periodic component analysis uses eigenvalue methods and interference to emphasize speech periodicity while avoiding long-delay, sampling-rate autocorrelation.

paragraphs: This paper develops reinforcement learning that explicitly accounts for disturbances and errors in environmental models. Models are useful for simulated learning and action planning, but disagreement between a model and the real environment can produce unwanted behavior. The proposed framework makes resistance to such disagreement part of the learning objective.

Drawing on H-infinity control, the authors formulate a differential game between an actor choosing control inputs and a disturber seeking the worst disturbance. A minimax value function considers both output deviation and disturbance magnitude. Online algorithms learn that value function and use it to calculate the control and disturbance choices.

Tests use an inverted pendulum. In the linear setting, the learned policy and value function coincide with analytical results from linear H-infinity theory. In a fully nonlinear swing-up task, the learned controller remains robust to changes in pendulum weight and friction, whereas the standard reinforcement-learning controller cannot handle those changes. The results connect agreement with established linear theory to robustness in the nonlinear task studied.
neurips-2000-robust-reinforcement-learni.tldr: A minimax reinforcement-learning controller matched linear control theory and handled weight and friction changes in a nonlinear pendulum task.

paragraphs: Noisy-OR networks represent situations where several possible causes can activate an outcome, but each cause may sometimes fail to do so. The abstract uses diseases and symptoms as an example. In richly connected networks, exact inference is intractable, creating a need for approximations to the distribution over hidden causes.

The paper focuses on a particular weakness of many approximations: they concentrate on a few likely configurations and overlook other plausible explanations. It introduces a sequential variational method for bipartite noisy-OR networks that represents the posterior as a tree. The method favors including all posterior modes, addressing the breadth of explanations retained by the approximation.

The authors compare the method with other approximations on an ensemble of networks whose statistics resemble those of the QMR-DT medical diagnostic network. The central contribution is an inclusive approach to posterior approximation: the fitting procedure is designed to retain competing explanations rather than concentrate too narrowly. The stated aim of including modes is a property the method favors, rather than a guarantee that every explanation is recovered.
neurips-2000-sequentially-fitting-inclus.tldr: Sequential tree-based variational inference is designed to preserve competing explanations in bipartite noisy-OR networks.

paragraphs: This paper seeks an information-theoretic explanation for synaptic changes that depend on the relative timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes. It starts from the principle of maximizing mutual information and derives a learning rule with temporal dependence. The resulting rule is then studied in relation to experimentally observed plasticity.

The authors find that a supervised, spike-dependent rule with a structure similar to the observed plasticity raises mutual information to a stable level near the optimum. This connects a specific learning objective with a timing-sensitive pattern of synaptic adaptation. The result concerns the derived supervised rule and its information behavior, while the structural similarity supplies the link to experimental observations.

The analysis also relates the timing structure of the learning rule to the temporal filter neurons apply to their inputs. This gives the model a connection to neuronal processing beyond spike timing alone. The authors suggest experimental predictions about how learning rules should depend on biophysical parameters, extending the account from an information objective to potentially testable dependencies.
neurips-2000-temporally-dependent-plasti.tldr: Mutual-information maximization yields a timing-dependent plasticity rule whose temporal structure is linked to neuronal input filtering.

paragraphs: The Kernel Gibbs Sampler explores the hypothesis space of kernel classifiers through Bayesian sampling. The setup assumes a uniform prior over normalized weight vectors and a likelihood based on label noise. Together, these choices produce a posterior density that is constant within separate regions of parameter space.

The algorithm exploits that structure with Markov chain Monte Carlo. It chooses a random direction in parameter space and samples from the piecewise constant density along the resulting line. Repeating this operation provides a way to explore the posterior over classifiers, making the label-noise model part of the inference procedure.

The authors present the sampler as an analytical tool for small datasets with noisy labels, with possible uses in Bayesian transduction, Bayes point machines, active learning, and evidence-based model selection. In a simple toy experiment, a Bayes point machine using the sampler outperforms an SVM that cannot account for label noise. That comparison illustrates the usefulness of explicitly representing noisy labels in the particular example studied.
neurips-2000-the-kernel-gibbs-sampler-42.tldr: The Kernel Gibbs Sampler samples noisy-label classifier posteriors through random-direction updates and supports Bayesian analysis of small datasets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a joint probabilistic model for a collection's document contents and the connections between its documents. Web pages and research-paper archives are the stated examples. The modeling task brings together what documents discuss and how they link to one another within a single representation of the collection.

The approach uses a probabilistic factor decomposition to identify principal topics and authoritative documents within those topics. This associates document authority with topical structure, allowing the model to describe both subject matter and the documents that hold authority in each subject area. It also maps relationships between topics to construct a predictive model of link content.

The authors identify applications including retrieval, search, topic identification, query disambiguation, focused crawling, web authoring, and bibliometric analysis. These applications share a need to interpret documents in the context of their relationships. The contribution is a unified modeling framework that exposes topics, topic-specific authority, and connections among topics as related aspects of a linked document collection.
neurips-2000-the-missing-link-a-probabil.tldr: A joint model of document content and links identifies topics, topic-specific authorities, and relationships among topics.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a particle filter based on sequential importance sampling. Its main change concerns the proposal distribution, which determines where candidate particles are drawn. The algorithm uses a bank of unscented filters to construct that distribution, placing the proposal mechanism at the center of the filtering method.

The authors emphasize two properties of the proposal: it uses the latest available information efficiently, and it can have heavy tails. These properties concern both how current evidence guides sampling and how probability extends away from the distribution's central region. The algorithm also includes resampling and may include Markov chain Monte Carlo steps.

The reported experiments show substantial improvements over standard particle filtering and other nonlinear filtering methods. The authors describe this empirical result as consistent with their theoretical convergence proof. The paper thus combines a new construction of the importance proposal, experimental comparisons, and a convergence result. The experimental performance claim and the proof provide different forms of support for the same filtering algorithm.
neurips-2000-the-unscented-particle-filt.tldr: Unscented filters construct informed, potentially heavy-tailed particle proposals, yielding substantial improvements in the reported filtering experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to combine outputs from several classifiers into a coherent inference that respects constraints. Its central application is identifying phrase structure. The issue is how individual classification decisions can jointly form a valid structured interpretation, rather than being considered only as separate predictions.

The authors develop two general approaches. The first extends hidden Markov models to support a rich observation structure and general classifiers for dependencies between states and observations. This provides a Markovian framework in which classifier outputs can contribute to sequential inference. The second approach extends constraint-satisfaction formalisms, providing another route for combining decisions under structural requirements.

For both approaches, the paper develops efficient combination algorithms and studies them experimentally in shallow parsing. The contribution brings together flexible local classifiers and mechanisms for making their outputs jointly consistent. Presenting both Markovian and constraint-based formulations also makes the combination problem explicit: successful phrase-structure inference requires a procedure for coordinating the available predictions with the constraints on the final interpretation.
neurips-2000-the-use-of-classifiers-in-s.tldr: Two efficient frameworks combine classifier outputs into constrained phrase-structure predictions using extended HMMs and constraint satisfaction.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to construct weak classifiers for boosting. It presents an algorithm producing a linear classifier with error guaranteed to be better than random guessing for any distribution on the data. The authors also state that this weak learner is not useful for learning in general, separating the stated guarantee from broader practical effectiveness.

Under reasonable conditions on the distribution, the construction becomes an effective weak learner for one-dimensional problems. Preliminary simulations suggest similar behavior in higher dimensions, and the abstract says recent theoretical bounds corroborate that suggestion. The higher-dimensional evidence is therefore presented more cautiously than the conditional result for one dimension.

The paper additionally improves convergence-rate bounds for generalization error in settings where empirical error can be made small. The authors connect this condition to the availability of weak learners whose performance is guaranteed to exceed random guessing. The contribution joins a classifier construction with an analysis of how such weak-learning guarantees support conclusions about boosting's generalization behavior.
neurips-2000-weak-learners-and-improved-.tldr: The paper constructs a weak linear learner with conditional effectiveness and improves boosting generalization bounds when empirical error can be small.

paragraphs: This paper asks why sparse representations arise in models of simple-cell receptive fields in primary visual cortex. Earlier optimal-encoding accounts required an additional sparsity constraint. That requirement suggested sparsity might need an explanation separate from the pressure to represent information optimally.

The author revisits the noise assumption behind that conclusion. The earlier work used an ad hoc noise model; this paper instead describes neurons as Poisson processes, which the author regards as more biologically plausible. Under that modeling choice, sparsity no longer has to be imposed as an extra constraint. The change in the account comes from how neuronal noise is represented.

The author interprets this result as evidence that sparsity can follow from evolutionary pressure toward optimal representation, without being an independently selected objective. The key modeling lesson is that conclusions about the need for a separate sparsity principle depend on the assumed noise process. The stated evolutionary conclusion is the author's interpretation of the result obtained with the Poisson-neuron model.
neurips-2000-whence-sparseness-318b325ff.tldr: With a Poisson model of neuronal noise, sparse representations emerge without an additional sparsity constraint.
